slot.brief: A man walks in rain falling vertically; find how umbrella angle changes when he runs faster, using relative-velocity vector construction.

stem: Rain falls vertically at $6$ m s$^{-1}$. A man walks horizontally at $2$ m s$^{-1}$ and holds his umbrella tilted at angle $\theta$ to the vertical. If he doubles his speed without changing the rain, by what factor does $\tan\theta$ change?

verdicts.working: The umbrella aligns with the rain’s velocity relative to the man, so \(\tan\theta=v/6\). Doubling the man’s speed doubles \(\tan\theta\); the factor is 2.

working:
$\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_{\text{man}}}{v_{\text{rain}}}$.
With $v_{\text{man}}$ doubled and $v_{\text{rain}}$ unchanged, $\tan\theta$ doubles.

Independent check: The umbrella aligns with the rain’s velocity relative to the man, so \(\tan\theta=v/6\). Doubling the man’s speed doubles \(\tan\theta\); the factor is 2.
solution:
The umbrella aligns with the rain’s velocity relative to the man, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_{\text{man}}}{v_{\text{rain}}}$. Since the rain speed is unchanged, doubling the man’s speed doubles $\tan\theta$.
$$\text{Factor change}=2$$
